evidence.citation: Chintu et al. 2004 (likely; author/year not provided in abstract)
evidence.population: Children aged 1–14 years in Zambia with clinical features of HIV infection; 541 randomized; 7 later found HIV-negative and excluded (thus HIV-infected children analyzed).
evidence.setting: Zambia; double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial conducted in a setting with high bacterial resistance to co-trimoxazole.
evidence.intervention: Daily co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole) prophylaxis; dosing/timing not specified in the abstract; administered throughout follow-up.

outcomes.outcome_name: All-cause mortality among those followed >12 months
Pneumocystis carinii (PCP) detection among pneumonia cases (NPA immunofluorescence)

evidence.follow_up: Median 19 months; subgroup analysis for those followed beyond 12 months (n=320).
adverse_events: Grade 3/4 adverse events: 16/≈? (6%) in co-trimoxazole vs 18/≈? (7%) in placebo.
Severe neutropenia on one occasion (<0.5×10^9/L): 16 (6%) co-trimoxazole vs 7 (3%) placebo; p=0.06.
Rash: 1 event reported in placebo group.
key_findings: Mortality significantly reduced with daily co-trimoxazole vs placebo: deaths 74 (co-trimoxazole) vs 112 (placebo); HR 0.57 (95% CI 0.43–0.77), p=0.0002.
Benefit persisted among children followed >12 months: HR 0.48 (95% CI 0.27–0.84); test for heterogeneity by follow-up duration p=0.60.
Effect consistent across ages (heterogeneity p=0.82) and baseline CD4 counts (heterogeneity p=0.36).
No excess in overall grade 3/4 adverse events (6% vs 7%); trend toward more transient severe neutropenia with co-trimoxazole (6% vs 3%; p=0.06).
PCP (Pneumocystis carinii) rarely identified: 1/73 nasopharyngeal aspirates positive (placebo group).
evidence.notes: Trial was stopped early on DSMC recommendation (Oct 2003). Analysis by intention-to-treat. Area had high background bacterial resistance to co-trimoxazole, but resistance outcomes were not reported. Dosing schedule not provided in abstract. Numerators for deaths provided (74 vs 112) but per-arm denominators not specified in abstract.

strengths: Large effect size on all-cause mortality with narrow confidence interval
Effect consistent across age and baseline CD4 strata
limitations: Trial stopped early by DSMC for benefit (potential to overestimate effect)
Allocation concealment and sequence generation methods not explicitly reported in abstract
Limited reporting on non-mortality clinical endpoints (bacterial infections, malaria, hospitalizations)
Antimicrobial resistance outcomes not measured or reported
Dose/regimen details not specified in abstract
risk_of_bias_concerns: Selective reporting possible for morbidity outcomes

synthesis: [1] In HIV-infected Zambian children (1–14 years), daily cotrimoxazole prophylaxis reduced all-cause mortality versus placebo over a median 19-month follow-up (HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.43–0.77), with a sustained benefit among those followed beyond 12 months (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.27–0.84). Effects were consistent across age and baseline CD4 strata. [1] Illness episodes: Pneumocystis pneumonia was rarely identified (1/73 NPAs, placebo arm), and the trial abstract did not report comparative rates for bacterial infections, malaria, or hospitalizations; thus morbidity effects beyond mortality remain uncertain. [1] Safety: Overall grade 3/4 adverse events were similar between arms (6% cotrimoxazole vs 7% placebo). There was a trend toward more transient severe neutropenia with cotrimoxazole (6% vs 3%; p=0.06), without an excess of other serious harms. Heterogeneity and applicability: Evidence derives from a single RCT in a low-resource, high–bacterial resistance setting (Zambia), using daily cotrimoxazole throughout follow-up. No data were available for HIV-exposed, uninfected infants. Outcome definitions for non-mortality morbidity were limited, and antimicrobial resistance emergence was not measured. Overall, the trial provides moderate-strength evidence that routine cotrimoxazole substantially reduces mortality in HIV-infected children in similar settings, with acceptable safety. Evidence is insufficient for effects on specific morbidity outcomes and for HIV-exposed infants.
limitations: Single RCT from one country; external validity to other contexts uncertain
Trial stopped early for benefit, which can overestimate treatment effects
Limited reporting on non-mortality morbidity outcomes (bacterial infections, malaria, hospital admissions)
No data for HIV-exposed, uninfected infants
No measurement/reporting of antimicrobial resistance emergence
Dose/regimen details not provided in the abstract
